content: A chemical burn occurs when living tissue comes into contact with a reactive chemical substance, such as a strong acid or base. The primary categories of irritant and/or corrosive substances include acids, bases, oxidizers, solvents, and reducing agents. When chemicals come into contact with the skin, they can cause localized reactions on the skin, systemic effects throughout the body, or both. It is important to note that chemical exposure is not always immediately apparent. If an otherwise healthy individual becomes ill without an obvious cause, and an empty chemical container is found nearby, chemical exposure should be considered as a potential cause. Prolonged exposure to chemicals in occupational settings can lead to cumulative effects, with symptoms evolving over time as the chemical accumulates in the body. Chemical burns are classified according to standard burn classification systems and can result in significant tissue damage. Certain sources, such as sparklers and other fireworks that emit sparks or flames, can cause chemical burns in addition to burns caused by heat. Other common agents responsible for chemical burns include silver nitrate (AgNO₃), hydrochloric acid (HCl), lye (NaOH), and lime (CaO). Chemical burns can occur through direct contact with body surfaces, such as the skin and eyes, as well as through inhalation or ingestion of the chemical substance. Occupations that involve chemical fabrication, mining, medicine, and related professional fields are associated with an increased risk of chemical burns due to the nature of the work and the potential for exposure to hazardous substances.
